summary: Defines how the Integrated Services controlled load and guaranteed services map onto low-bitrate links.

eli5.summary: How to reserve a bit of a slow road for important traffic so it is not stuck.

questions: controlled load guaranteed service slow links
how does intserv work on low speed links
what is the d error term in guaranteed service
subtitle: Guidelines for giving reserved, low-delay service to some flows on slow modem, ISDN and sub-T1 links.

tldr.problem: Integrated Services promise special treatment for some flows, but on slow point-to-point links one large best-effort packet can hold up a time-sensitive packet for too long.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC maps controlled load and guaranteed service onto PPP classes, using either fragmentation or suspend/resume, and gives rules for admission control, the delay error term D, and the effect of bit and byte stuffing.
tldr.outcome: It is a set of guidelines and evaluation criteria rather than a new wire format. Proposed Standard; the metadata lists no replacement.

facts.label: Links covered
facts.value: Dial-up, ISDN, leased lines of 1.5Mbps or less

today: RFC 2688 is a Proposed Standard, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It remains a set of guidelines to be read together with the companion documents it cites, such as RFC 2689.

sections.title: Integrated Services on Slow Links
sections.content:
Beyond ordinary best-effort delivery, the Internet is gaining integrated services: special handling of traffic based on bandwidth, latency and other needs that best effort cannot usually meet. RFC 2688 defines how two of those services, controlled load (RFC 2211) and guaranteed service (RFC 2212), map onto low-bandwidth links.

The architecture and mechanisms live in companion documents. They include compression of flows to save bandwidth and PPP extensions that either fragment large packets (RFC 2686) or suspend them (RFC 2687) in favour of flows with stricter needs. This RFC takes the form of guidelines, considerations and evaluation criteria for implementing the two services on top of those mechanisms. It uses the RFC 2119 key words.
sections.eli5: Some traffic, like a phone call, cannot wait in line. This paper explains how to give that traffic a fast pass on a slow connection.

sections.title: Slow Links: Fragmentation or Suspend/Resume
sections.content:
The links covered are low speed point-to-point connections: dial-up lines, ISDN channels and leased lines of 1.5Mbps or less. They can sit at the end of a host, between a host and an access device, between edge devices, or rarely between backbone routers. They are often the first or last wide-area hop and may be the most bandwidth-constrained part of the path.

The services only work if both ends of the link support the architecture, which is determined during PPP negotiation. Because the links are not shared and are typically dual simplex, all admission control decisions can be made locally.

There are two ways to keep a long packet from delaying an urgent one. With suspend/resume, a best-effort packet in flight is preempted when a packet for an admitted flow arrives, the urgent data is sent, and the best-effort packet then resumes, usually in one transmission. The receiver separates the pieces. With fragmentation, packets longer than the tolerable delay are cut up beforehand so a short packet can be interleaved between fragments. Suspend/resume saves header overhead and can give better delay, but needs all outgoing data prepared and all incoming data scanned for control information. Fragmentation needs no extra scanning and suits systems that only control whole frames. This is multilink PPP fragmentation, local to the link, not IP fragmentation, so it does not affect the end-to-end MTU.
sections.eli5: You can either pause a long train to let an ambulance cross, or cut the long train into short pieces ahead of time. Pausing is neat but needs careful watching, and cutting is simpler.

sections.title: Deciding What Delay Is Acceptable
sections.content:
A router must have some idea of how much delay it may add before starting to send a packet from an int-serv flow. With fragmentation it needs a fragment size; with suspend/resume it needs to know when suspending is appropriate. There is no hard and fast way to derive a per-hop delay from a reservation, because endpoints do not communicate a per-hop delay to routers.

For guaranteed service, a network operator can configure the link so that the rate-independent error term D takes a chosen value. With fragmentation, the configured fragment size gives one component of D: the time to send one fragment. With suspend/resume, a delay parameter is configured instead.

Controlled load has no error terms. A flow with token bucket rate r should see something like an unloaded network of capacity r, so packets should not see end-to-end delay much beyond b/r plus propagation. The router should add substantially less than b/r, though that is hard for flows with very small b. Making the delay too small costs fragmentation overhead; making D too large may stop applications from making a reservation that meets their goals.
sections.eli5: Nobody tells the router exactly how long it may make a packet wait, so the owner picks a limit. A smaller limit is faster but wastes more effort on cutting things up.

sections.title: Mapping Services to PPP Classes
sections.content:
The multi-class PPP formats offer a small number of classes: MCML short sequence numbers give 2 bits of class (four classes), MCML long sequence numbers give 4 bits, and the real-time framing (RTF) gives 3 bits. The RFC describes three ways to use them.

Predefined mappings (3.1) put admitted flows into a few buckets of service level, as in Table 1 of the RFC. Flows in one bucket are scheduled against each other per packet, not per fragment, which can make admission control overly conservative when few classes exist, as with the MCML short format. Predefined mappings with prefix elision (3.2) assign known flows to fixed classes when fewer reservations are expected than classes negotiated, so that prefix elision can save a little bandwidth.

Dynamic mappings (3.3) assign a class per packet. The class number MUST stay constant for all fragments of one packet, but MAY change from packet to packet. Classes need no meaning beyond identifying which fragments belong to one packet, so several flows MAY share a class. Best-effort traffic SHOULD be logically separated from QoS traffic and mapped to a fragmentable class (MCML 0-3 short, 0-15 long) or a suspendable one (RTF 0-6); class 0 is a natural choice.

For non-conformant traffic (3.4), policing SHOULD work per packet: drop whole packets, never individual fragments. If such traffic is forwarded when bandwidth allows, it SHOULD be fragmented as if best effort.
sections.eli5: The road has only a few lanes. You can give each kind of car a fixed lane, or hand out lanes one car at a time, as long as every piece of one car stays in the same lane.

sections.title: Admission Control and the D Error Term
sections.content:
Admission control MUST decide whether to admit a flow based on rate and delay. It first works out the effective size of an MTU-sized packet after compression (CMTU) and after fragmentation with headers (eMTU), then the effective rate eRate = eMTU/CMTU * R, where R is the requested rate. For controlled load it MUST compute CMTU, eMTU and eRate; for guaranteed service it MUST also compute D. Admission control SHOULD compare eRate with the remaining bandwidth.

A controlled load flow can be admitted if there is enough bandwidth after that calculation and enough buffer space (the sum of the token bucket sizes must not exceed buffer capacity). The RFC warns that statistical multiplexing is risky on low-bitrate links because delay from a temporary overcommitment is hard to amortize.

For guaranteed service the rate-dependent term C needs no special treatment, while D is the inherent link delay Dlink plus the worst-case delay of one more fragment or of suspend/resume overhead. Dlink may be configured by an administrative tool, measured, or taken from hardware or PPP negotiation.
sections.eli5: Before letting a new traveller onto a narrow bridge, you count how much room they really take up once their baggage is included, and check the bridge still has space.

sections.title: Stuffing, Compression and Scheduling
sections.content:
Stuffing. Bit stuffing can add as much as 20% overhead, so admission control for guaranteed service over such links SHOULD multiply the RSpec rate of all flows by 1.2. Byte stuffing, common on POTS modems using v.42, can in the worst case double frame sizes, so a strict implementation SHOULD double the RSpec. Controlled load implementations MAY measure average expansion or MAY use the theoretical worst case.

Compression. When deciding to admit a flow, admission control MUST account for header compression (Van Jacobson or Casner-Jacobson), prefix elision, CCP, the fragment header option in use, and fragmentation versus suspend/resume. Compression and elision gains MUST be included.

Scheduling. The link-level scheduler fragments packets, maps them to classes and schedules among classes. With dynamic mapping, packets with the tightest delay needs should not be put in a class where large packets are being sent. The scheduler SHOULD control how much bandwidth each class gets, in line with the sum of reservations of flows currently using it.
sections.eli5: Packing tape and extra wrapping make a parcel bigger than it looks, so you must count that extra when you decide how many parcels fit on the truck.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
General security issues of multilink PPP and PPP are covered in RFC 1990 and RFC 1661, and those of RSVP in RFC 2209. One specific issue arises here: if admission control relies on observed or theoretical average expansion from bit or byte stuffing, an adversary could deliberately send traffic that causes worst-case expansion. Other flows could then miss their quality of service guarantees because admission was too permissive. The RFC argues strongly for a worst-case expansion factor, even for controlled load.

Otherwise it introduces no new security issues beyond the companion documents, and assumes all requests for service are authenticated appropriately.
sections.eli5: A troublemaker could stuff parcels with air to make them swell, so plan for the biggest swelling rather than the average.

sections.title: Admission Control Over POTS Modems
sections.content:
Appendix A warns that POTS modems can change link rate and delay during a call, and admission control and scheduling MUST be prepared for that. The v.34 protocol adapts to line conditions, and typically raises the rate by about 10% in the first minute, though decreases are possible. Implementations MUST gracefully handle the case where the rate falls below the capacity already reserved.

Delay often does not settle. The v.42 protocol provides reliability by retransmission, which delays frames and steals bandwidth, making a guaranteed service reservation extremely difficult to honour. Controlled load can tolerate this on a lightly or moderately loaded link, but becomes hard to offer at high utilization when retransmissions occur.
sections.eli5: A wobbly phone line can get slower or faster while you use it, so promises about speed must be made with care.

data.title: Admission control formulas
data.code:
#_of_Fragments = CMTU div (FRAG-Header)
Last_Frag_Size = CMTU mod (FRAG-Header)

If Last_Frag_Size != 0
   eMTU = (#_of_Fragments) * FRAG + Last_Frag_Size + Header
Else
   eMTU = (#_of_Fragments) * FRAG

eRate = eMTU/CMTU * R

D = Dlink + FRAG/LinkRate          (fragmentation)
D = Dlink + pHeader + pDelay       (suspend/resume)
